opus-5.5.text:
I think the gap is real, but it's often misunderstood. People tend to imagine it as a pure capability gap, as if the question were just "is model A better than model B on some benchmark." In an agent setting, that's only part of the story.

When the three models are trained and designed together, the biggest advantage is **consistency**. They share assumptions about how a task is broken down, how intermediate results are represented, and what a "good handoff" looks like between steps. Say one model is doing the reasoning and planning, another handles perception or multimodal input, and another is optimized for speed or tool execution. If they come from the same training philosophy and similar data distributions, the outputs of one fit naturally into the inputs of the next. You lose much less information at the seams.

When you assemble models from different providers, each one can be very strong individually. But every model has its own habits: how verbose it is, how it formats things, how it interprets an ambiguous instruction, how confident it sounds when it's actually unsure. In a single-turn chat that barely matters. In a long agent loop with dozens or hundreds of steps, those small mismatches compound. You end up writing a lot of glue logic, prompts, and parsing just to make them understand each other, and that glue becomes its own source of errors.

The second point is **cost and latency as a design dimension**. If you control all three models, you can decide which part of the pipeline deserves the expensive reasoning and which part should be fast and cheap, and you can co-optimize them. With a mixed setup you're more or less stuck with whatever trade-offs each provider has made.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. For many developers, mixing models is completely reasonable, especially if there's one provider that's clearly best at a specific capability they care about. The ecosystem benefits from that kind of openness too. Our view is more that, as agents get longer-horizon and more autonomous, the value of models that were *meant* to work together grows. It shifts from a nice-to-have to something that really affects whether the task finishes reliably at all.

So I'd say: on short, simple tasks the gap is small, sometimes negligible. On complex, long-chain agent tasks, the integration advantage is where we see the most meaningful difference, and that's the direction we're betting on.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap is small on short, simple tasks, but describes a meaningful integration advantage on complex, long-chain agent tasks. It does not state that the current overall gap is very slight.

r002.rationale: The response expects the advantage of models designed to work together to grow as agents become longer-horizon and more autonomous, making the gap more consequential.

fable-5.1.text:
When you build the three models in one house, the biggest difference is not any single benchmark. It is that we control the whole data pipeline and the whole training loop, so the models learn to work with each other rather than merely coexisting behind an API.

Let me explain concretely. When you assemble an agent from several providers, you are stitching together models that were never trained to expect each other. The planner produces an output format, the vision model interprets instructions in its own way, the speech model has its own latency profile and its own failure modes. You end up writing a lot of glue, a lot of prompt engineering, a lot of retry logic, just to paper over the mismatches. And every time one provider ships an update, the glue breaks somewhere, and you may not even find out until users complain.

With our own models, we can design the interfaces at training time. The trajectories that the agent produces, including the mistakes, the tool calls, the moments where vision input changes the plan, go back into training for all three. So the language model learns what the vision model is actually good at and bad at, and asks it the right questions. The speech side learns the rhythm of the agent's thinking, when to interrupt, when to wait. That kind of co-adaptation you simply cannot get across company boundaries, because nobody will share their training data or their reward signals with you.

The second point is cost and latency. In an agent framework you might make dozens of calls per task. If each call goes to a different vendor with a different serving stack, the latency adds up, and so does the bill. On our side we can co-locate the models, share KV caches where it makes sense, and decide which steps truly need the large model and which can be handled by something small and fast. That is an engineering decision we can make end to end.

But I want to be honest about the gap in the other direction. The strongest frontier model from the best lab, on a given day, is probably better at raw reasoning than ours. If you only care about the hardest step in your pipeline and nothing else, assembling from the best of each provider can win on that step. So the question we ask ourselves is not whether we beat every model on every leaderboard. It is whether the whole system, trained together, deployed together, iterated together, delivers a better and more reliable experience to the user, especially on devices where we know exactly the hardware, the scenes, and the user's intent.

For the kinds of products we are building, I think the answer is yes, and the advantage widens over time because the feedback loop is ours. For a research team that just wants to prototype quickly with the best components available, mixing providers is still a perfectly reasonable choice. The two approaches are optimizing for different things.

r001.rationale: The response compares the approaches but does not say their current gap in potential is very slight.

r002.rationale: It says the advantage of the internally trained system widens over time, but does not clearly state that the future gap will no longer be slight.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between models that work well individually and models that work well together. In an agent framework, the handoffs matter: does one model understand what another has already done, what remains uncertain, and when to take over?

Using our three models together gives us the opportunity to optimize those interactions as a whole. When you assemble models from different providers, you have more flexibility to choose the strongest model for each task, but the framework has to handle differences in their behavior and interfaces.

That said, being from the same provider doesn’t automatically make the combination better. You still have to demonstrate that it completes tasks more reliably, at an acceptable cost and latency. That’s where I would measure the gap—not simply in whether the models come from us or someone else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible benefits and tradeoffs but does not state that the current gap is very slight.

r002.rationale: The response makes no prediction that the gap will grow or stop being slight in the future.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real difference is how well the models work together, rather than simply whether they come from the same provider. In an agent framework, one model’s output becomes another model’s input, so the handoff matters: what information gets passed along, how uncertainty is communicated, and how errors are caught.

Using our three models together gives us more control over those interactions. But that advantage has to show up in the results. If someone assembles models from different providers and gets better task completion, lower latency, or lower cost, that’s a strong system too.

So I wouldn’t say that putting three models together automatically creates an advantage. The question is whether we can optimize the whole workflow so that they solve problems together more reliably than they could individually. That’s the gap we need to demonstrate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible advantages and says they must be demonstrated, but does not state that the current gap is very slight.

r002.rationale: The response says the gap needs to be demonstrated, but does not express an expectation that it will stop being slight in the future.
